name: Consensus
intent: Get several machines to agree on the same sequence of values even when some crash or messages are lost, so that a replicated system behaves like a single reliable one.
scenario: Three or five servers each hold a copy of a configuration store. A client writes 'x = 7'. Once the client is told 'done', that write must survive any minority of crashes, and every server must apply writes in the same order.
problem: Replicas must apply the same operations in the same order, or they diverge. But machines crash at any moment, messages are delayed or lost, and no machine can tell whether another is dead or merely slow. A famous result (FLP) shows that perfect agreement with no timing assumptions is impossible, so practical algorithms assume partial synchrony (the network is usually, not always, on time) and require a majority to make progress.

howItWorks.title: Replicate a log, not just a value
howItWorks.text: Instead of agreeing on one value, nodes agree on an ordered log of commands ('set x=7', 'set y=3'). If every node applies the same log in the same order, they all end in the same state. This idea is called a replicated state machine.

howItWorks.title: The leader appends and replicates
howItWorks.text: A client sends a command to the leader. The leader appends it to its own log and sends it to the followers (AppendEntries in Raft). Followers append it and acknowledge. At this point the entry is stored but not yet decided.

howItWorks.title: An entry is committed once a majority has it
howItWorks.text: When the leader knows that a majority of nodes (3 of 5) have stored the entry, it is committed: it can never be lost, because any future leader must have been elected by a majority that overlaps with this one. The leader applies it, answers the client, and tells followers to apply it too.

howItWorks.title: The leader changes, and the log is repaired
howItWorks.text: If the leader crashes, a new one is elected, and Raft only allows a node with an up-to-date log to win. Entries that were committed are always present on the new leader. Entries that were not committed may be discarded, and the leader overwrites any follower's conflicting entries so all logs converge.

howItWorks.title: Fault tolerance and its price
howItWorks.text: A cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures: 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2. Without a majority the system stops accepting writes rather than risk disagreement, which is the consistency side of the CAP trade-off. Every write costs at least one round trip to a majority, so consensus is used for small, critical data, not bulk traffic.

pros: Strong consistency: all nodes see the same order of writes
Committed data survives the failure of a minority of nodes
Automatic recovery with no data loss for committed writes
A building block for databases, coordination services and metadata stores
cons: Writes need a majority round trip, so latency and throughput are limited
No progress without a majority: a minority partition is read-only or unavailable
Complex to implement correctly, with many subtle cases
Does not scale writes by adding nodes: more nodes means more to replicate
whenToUse: Metadata, configuration, locks and leader leases (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul)
Replicated databases that need strong consistency (Spanner, CockroachDB, etcd)
Any place where split brain (two groups each acting as leader) or lost committed writes would be unacceptable
whenNotToUse: High-volume data paths where eventual consistency is acceptable
Implementing it yourself when a proven service or library will do
Across slow wide-area links without understanding the latency cost
pitfalls: Running an even number of nodes and expecting extra fault tolerance
Putting large or frequent writes through the consensus log
Placing all nodes in one failure domain, such as one rack or one zone
Treating a write as durable before it is committed by a majority

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends commands and waits for a commit.

roles.label: Leader
roles.description: Orders commands and replicates the log.

roles.label: Follower
roles.description: Stores the log and applies committed entries.

quiz.question: In a 5-node Raft cluster, the leader appends 'x = 7' to its own log and to one follower, then crashes before any other node gets it. The client has not yet been told 'done'. What is the status of that entry?
options: It is committed, because the leader and a follower both stored it and the leader had accepted the command.
It is committed, because a node with the entry is always chosen as the new leader.
It is committed once the crashed leader restarts, because a leader's log is never overwritten.
It is not committed, because only 2 of 5 nodes have it, and a new leader may discard it.
quiz.explanation: An entry is committed only when a majority, 3 of 5, has it. With 2 copies the entry is not safe, and a new leader can overwrite it, which is fine because the client was never acknowledged. The new leader can be a node without the entry, and a restarted old leader has its uncommitted entries overwritten.

quiz.question: A team runs a 3-node etcd cluster and adds a fourth node, expecting to tolerate more failures. How many node failures can the 4-node cluster survive?
options: Two, because half of 4 nodes is enough to continue.
One, the same as three nodes, because a majority of 4 is 3.
Two, because the extra node can stand by and take over.
Three, because one surviving node can continue alone.
quiz.explanation: A majority of 4 is 3, so losing 2 nodes stops writes, exactly as in a 3-node cluster. Odd sizes give the most tolerance per machine. A standby adds no vote, and one node alone could disagree with the rest.

quiz.question: A 5-node consensus cluster has 3 nodes in zone A and 2 nodes in zone B. Zone A loses power completely. What happens, and what layout would avoid it?
options: Zone B elects a leader with its 2 nodes and carries on, with the other 3 nodes catching up later.
Zone B stays up and accepts reads and writes, because the 2 nodes agree with one another.
Zone B's 2 nodes cannot form a majority, so writes stop. Use three zones, such as 2, 2 and 1.
Writes continue in zone B, and no layout is needed, because consensus tolerates the loss of one zone.
quiz.explanation: Writes need 3 of 5 votes, and zone B only has 2. If it carried on alone it could diverge from zone A, which is what consensus prevents. Spreading nodes over failure domains means losing one zone still leaves a majority.
